prompt:
A 42-year-old woman presents for evaluation of newly elevated cholesterol. Her history includes a corticotroph adenoma treated with transsphenoidal surgery two years ago (now on hydrocortisone 10 mg daily), an abnormal glucagon stimulation test suggesting growth hormone deficiency (managed with an over-the-counter supplement per her preference), SIBO/IMO, and osteoporosis. Despite a reasonably healthy diet, her LDL cholesterol has risen markedly compared with normal lipids one year ago. She lives with her spouse and two children.

One year ago: total cholesterol 180 mg/dL; HDL 55 mg/dL; LDL 95 mg/dL; triglycerides 120 mg/dL.
One week ago: total cholesterol 245 mg/dL; HDL 50 mg/dL; LDL 160 mg/dL; triglycerides 140 mg/dL.

What may be the etiology of the hyperlipidemia?

Provide a comprehensive management plan including appropriate diagnostic workup, referrals, procedures if indicated, follow-up, and actions to avoid.

rubric_items.text: Recognize the abrupt LDL rise after previously normal lipids as favoring a secondary cause over monogenic familial hypercholesterolemia.
Evaluate central hypothyroidism and inadequately treated adult growth hormone deficiency as leading endocrine causes of the dyslipidemia.
Review all prescription medications and over-the-counter supplements for lipid-raising effects.
Repeat a lipid panel in approximately 6–12 weeks to confirm persistent dyslipidemia; fasting is optional at this triglyceride level.
Order TSH and free T4 to evaluate for hypothyroidism, interpreting free T4 as the key test for central hypothyroidism.
Order hemoglobin A1c to screen for diabetes or prediabetes.
Order a comprehensive metabolic panel including hepatic and renal function.
Order a urine albumin-to-creatinine or protein-to-creatinine ratio to evaluate for nephrotic-range protein loss.
Review hydrocortisone dose and timing for evidence of glucocorticoid over-replacement.
Coordinate adrenal-axis testing with endocrinology to account for hydrocortisone interference.
Order serum IGF-1 as part of reassessment for adult growth hormone deficiency.
Confirm growth hormone deficiency with an endocrinology-supervised glucagon stimulation test or insulin tolerance test.
Review pituitary tumor surveillance and arrange pituitary MRI if surveillance is due or new clinical, biochemical, or pituitary-function findings warrant imaging.
Refer to endocrinology for comprehensive reassessment of pituitary hormone replacement.
Advise discontinuation of the over-the-counter growth hormone supplement or secretagogue because it is not adequate replacement.
Discuss FDA-approved recombinant growth hormone replacement if adult growth hormone deficiency is confirmed.
Calculate the 10-year ASCVD risk and review risk-enhancing factors before selecting lipid-lowering therapy.
Counsel on a Mediterranean-style diet low in saturated fat.
Recommend regular aerobic physical activity.
Refer to a registered dietitian for medical nutrition therapy.

After addressing secondary causes, reassess LDL and cardiovascular risk and use shared decision-making to determine whether lipid-lowering medication is indicated; if so, offer an appropriate-intensity statin.
Arrange follow-up in 6–8 weeks to review endocrine testing and the repeat lipid panel.
Initiate high-intensity statin therapy before evaluating the abrupt change for secondary causes.
Use a PCSK9 inhibitor as first-line therapy for this presentation.
Initiate recombinant growth hormone empirically without endocrinology reassessment.
Recommend continuing the over-the-counter growth hormone product as adequate treatment.
Empirically increase hydrocortisone to treat the dyslipidemia.
Start levothyroxine without checking free T4 and ensuring adrenal-axis safety.
Use a fibrate as primary therapy for the elevated LDL and triglycerides of 140 mg/dL.
Prescribe niacin for LDL reduction.
Use ezetimibe monotherapy before addressing secondary endocrine causes.
Prescribe red yeast rice as the primary lipid-lowering treatment.
Recommend a diet high in saturated fat as treatment for the LDL elevation.
Order familial hypercholesterolemia genetic testing as the initial evaluation despite previously normal LDL.
Order coronary artery calcium scoring or coronary CT angiography as the initial diagnostic step for the lipid elevation.
Perform invasive coronary angiography for asymptomatic LDL elevation.
Recommend aspirin for primary prevention solely because the LDL is elevated.
Refer for LDL apheresis for this degree of LDL elevation.
Prescribe estrogen hormone therapy to treat the hyperlipidemia.
Discontinue necessary glucocorticoid replacement without alternative glucocorticoid coverage or documented recovery of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis.
